source_text: That works for me. We could do this for any set of turns, but it occurs to me that if we added a slight "delay" to the pipeline, we could do this "live", e.g. by sending from operator to  象  to agent so that the agent would get the pattern-interpreted turns and could adjust their intents accordingly.  That becomes a bit mind bending so maybe we won't do it live right away.

reply_text:
Starting step 1, writing the flow as Agency events. Your live-pipeline idea is answered at the end.㊥ (step 1 result) I ran the flow through the Agency skeleton, with your two `🈸:yes` turns included. I checked two versions. In the first, every 🈸 is a question that was actually sent; in the second, only what the offer route recorded. Both pass all of the skeleton's laws, but they differ where it matters:
- **As spoken,** the only unanswered question is C3's "Shall I?". J2's "No" counts as an answer to C1's corpus ask, so that ask was declined, not a dead end as I said last time.
- **As recorded,** your two `🈸:yes` turns answer questions the record doesn't contain.

The skeleton doesn't flag that second case. It assumes such a question was asked before the window began, so my prediction of two `:ill-typed` findings was wrong.

㊢ (what I did) The probe is `holes/labs/M-diagramprover/flow_23519_agency_probe.clj` (commit `7c1bda7f`). It writes each turn as Agency events:
- your turns are requests to me;
- my 🈸 paragraphs are questions to you;
- the codex-10 request is a request to codex-10, which publishes the narration that C3 reads.

🈖 (what the gap means) The skeleton reads an unknown question as "asked before the window". That's the right default for a ledger excerpt, but it can't tell "asked earlier" from "never asked". To catch your refused agreements, the window would need to say "nothing before this point", so that any answer without its question is a finding. That's a small addition: a flag on `ingest` that turns those inputs into a finding. It's the same thing the mission's response projector needs, an explicit statement that no response arrived. I haven't made the change.

㊟ (the live version) Your pipeline, operator → 象 → agent, would make 象's reading of your turn, including the patterns it accepted or rejected, part of what I receive. I could then choose my marks knowing how the turn was read. In these models that adds one act between each J and C, which is easy to represent. It's harder to reason about, because my marks would then partly answer 象 rather than you. Holding it back is sensible. If it happens later, this flow, re-run with that extra act, shows what changes.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I add the "nothing before this point" flag to `ingest`, with a test? That would turn the `🈸:yes` refusals into findings the skeleton reports.

previous_reply_acts.text: (glyphs as decorations) Yes, with one adjustment. A glyph fits Fong's decorations when it's read as a set of intents attached to each act, merged by union when two theories are glued; that is a lawful decoration. But some glyphs also decide what shape the act's model has, and that does more than a decoration does. 🈸 opens an output that waits for an answer, which is exactly the Agency skeleton's bell, an open port until answered. 🈘 redirect and 🈡 withdraw act like interventions on a later act. So the glyphs work at two levels: decorations that come along through gluing, and types that constrain the mechanism. The second level is what makes them checkable.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (the decoration reading) In a decorated cospan, the apex carries structure F(N) for a functor F that pushes forward along the gluing map. "Each node gets a set of marks", F(N) = N → P(Marks), is such a functor: when gluing identifies nodes, their mark sets are joined by union. In our flow, each variable has one owning act, so the union never actually merges two acts' marks. A glyph comes along with its act unchanged, and the joined model keeps J1's "explore/propose" next to C1's "report/ask". That's the cheap, lawful version, and the flow probe could carry it as metadata today.

claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (bringing patterns back in) A pattern can't simply be glued onto the flow. If `disconfirmation-not-just-triangulation` is written as a theory ("two accounts, and their divergence, give a finding"), it claims the same variable C3 owns, the six-node table. `glue` refuses that as `:double-mechanism`. The right relation is refinement: the pattern's mechanism should be an abstraction of the act's mechanism. The Agency skeleton has a `refines?` check, but only for its queue-to-protocol rewriting. For causal theories it would mean mapping the act's variables onto the pattern's and checking the pattern's mechanism still holds. Each check would then give a definite answer, "C3 carries out this pattern" or "it doesn't". That's the pattern reference agent turns lack, computed rather than asserted.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(order, if you want to take it further)
1. **Agency events.** Write the flow's acts as Agency events, including both `🈸:yes` turns, and run `agency/check`. The expected findings are two `:ill-typed` answers and two open ports. That's small and uses only existing code.
2. **Decorations.** Carry intents as decorations in the flow probe and add the type constraints for 🈸 (the act must open a port) and ㊬ (the act needs a verification act behind it).
3. **Refinement.** Write one refinement check, for the disconfirmation pattern against C3.
